prompt_free_text:
This paper addresses an important and underexplored aspect of motion forecasting for autonomous driving: the fact that forecasting is performed continuously over time rather than as isolated one-shot predictions on independently sampled scenes. The central idea is to reorganize standard forecasting datasets into temporally ordered sub-scenes and to build a recurrent forecasting framework, RealMotion, with two temporal streams: a scene-context stream that propagates scene-level information across successive sub-scenes, and an agent-trajectory stream that relays prior predictions through a memory bank to refine current forecasts. The paper reports strong results on Argoverse 1 and 2, including leaderboard numbers on Argoverse 2, and argues that the method is both more realistic and more efficient for online deployment.

Overall, I find the problem formulation compelling. The mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment is real, and the paper’s emphasis on continuous driving is timely and practically meaningful. The proposed decomposition into scene-context accumulation and trajectory relaying is intuitive, and the empirical gains over the authors’ independent baseline are substantial. The paper is also ambitious in that it introduces not only a model but also a data reorganization protocol intended to bridge the benchmark-to-deployment gap. These are meaningful contributions.

That said, while the paper is promising, I have several concerns regarding novelty relative to prior temporal/streaming forecasting work, methodological clarity, fairness of comparisons, and the extent to which the reported gains can be attributed specifically to the proposed temporal modeling rather than to altered supervision/data construction. I believe the paper could become significantly stronger with clearer positioning, tighter experimental controls, and more rigorous analysis of what exactly is gained by the continuous formulation.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the motivation. The authors correctly point out that most forecasting methods operate on independently sampled scenes and discard temporal continuity across repeated forecasting calls. This is indeed a limitation if the goal is deployment in an autonomous driving stack. The paper also gives a plausible qualitative example involving occlusion and accumulated context. This framing is easy to appreciate and likely to resonate with the community. In addition, the architecture is reasonably lightweight, and the latency discussion is useful. The ablations indicate that both the scene-context stream and the trajectory stream contribute, and the gains over the independent variant are nontrivial.

However, the paper somewhat overstates the novelty of the setting and method without sufficiently distinguishing itself from prior work on temporal or streaming forecasting. The related work mentions Pang et al. on streaming motion forecasting, but the comparison is brief and not very informative. Since the paper’s main claim is that prior methods ignore temporal continuity, it is essential to carefully discuss what prior streaming/temporal formulations already exist, how RealMotion differs conceptually and technically, and whether the proposed data reorganization is fundamentally new or mainly a practical way to retrofit existing datasets. As written, the paper risks giving the impression that it is the first to consider temporally linked forecasting scenes, which the cited prior work already challenges. A more precise positioning would help.

A major methodological issue is that the data reorganization changes the training and evaluation setup in a way that may itself provide additional supervision or easier optimization. The paper splits each original scene into multiple sub-scenes with overlapping history/future windows and backpropagates through all segments. This effectively increases the number of training instances and introduces highly correlated supervision. The ablation in Table 4 shows that “continuous data” alone already yields a noticeable gain over the independent baseline, even without either temporal stream. This is important: it suggests that a meaningful fraction of the improvement may come from the reorganized data and denser supervision rather than from the recurrent temporal modeling itself. The paper acknowledges this as “extends dataset at no extra cost,” but this is precisely why stronger controls are needed. For example, one would want to compare against an independent baseline trained with the same number of effective samples or gradient steps, but without temporal state propagation. Otherwise, the gains are not cleanly attributable.

Relatedly, the comparison to external baselines on official leaderboards is difficult to interpret fairly because those methods were not trained or evaluated under the same reorganized continuous protocol. If RealMotion benefits from a transformed training distribution and repeated forecasting over sub-scenes, then leaderboard superiority does not isolate architectural merit. This does not invalidate the results, but it does mean the claims should be phrased more carefully. The fairest comparison is the one against RealMotion-I, and even there the paper should ensure that training budget, number of optimization steps, and exposure to reorganized samples are matched when isolating the effect of the streams.

I also found the technical description insufficiently precise in several places. The scene-context stream aligns historical scene features using MLN conditioned on relative pose and time, but it is not fully clear how correspondence is handled across scenes when the set of agents and map elements changes. Equation (2) repartitions aligned scene features into agent and map parts, but if the number or identity of agents differs across sub-scenes, what exactly is being aligned? Is the attention simply over unordered sets after pose normalization, or is there any identity-aware matching? If it is purely set-based, then the wording “align” may be stronger than what is actually done. Similar ambiguity appears in the trajectory stream: the memory bank is maintained per agent of interest, but in multi-agent forecasting there are many agents. How are identities maintained across sub-scenes, especially for appearing/disappearing agents? What happens when an agent is absent in some segment? How large is the memory bank in practice, and how are entries selected when multiple modes exist over multiple past timestamps?

The trajectory relaying mechanism is interesting, but its formulation raises questions. The paper argues that directly decoding from historical memory features is inappropriate because future motion patterns vary significantly in local coordinates, so instead it refines current predictions using memory trajectories. This is sensible. But the memory bank stores predicted trajectories rather than ground truth during inference, which introduces the possibility of error accumulation and confirmation bias. The paper does not analyze this failure mode. Under what conditions does relaying prior predictions help rather than hurt? Are there scenarios where an early wrong mode dominates later refinements? The ablations show average gains, but a more diagnostic analysis would be valuable, especially because recurrent prediction systems are often vulnerable to drift.

The evaluation protocol also needs clarification. The paper distinguishes “offline” and “online” latency, and states that for the offline dataset only the final prediction is used for evaluation, whereas in online application each iteration is meaningful. This is reasonable, but it also means the benchmark evaluation may not fully reflect the claimed practical advantage. If the method is designed for continuous forecasting, then a more convincing evaluation would report metrics over all forecasting calls in a sequence, not only the final one. For example, one could measure average forecasting error across all sub-scenes, temporal consistency of predictions, calibration over time, or robustness under occlusion. As it stands, the paper mainly evaluates the final sub-scene on standard one-shot metrics, which only partially validates the continuous-driving thesis.

The latency comparison is useful but not entirely apples-to-apples. RealMotion offline is reported at 62 ms versus QCNet at 94 ms, but RealMotion online is 20 ms and HPTR online is 13 ms. Since the paper’s main deployment claim concerns continuous online use, the online comparison should be emphasized and made as fair as possible. It would help to specify exactly what is cached, what preprocessing is included, whether map encoding is reused, and whether the same hardware/software stack is used for all methods. The current presentation leaves some uncertainty about how comparable these numbers are.

Another concern is that the paper’s strongest empirical claims rely heavily on Argoverse 2 leaderboard results, but the methodological novelty is not fully stress-tested beyond that benchmark. Since the authors themselves note that existing datasets provide limited historical information and that their approach is constrained by sufficient history length, it would be useful to evaluate more directly how performance scales with available temporal context. The split-point ablation is a start, but it is somewhat narrow. A more informative study would vary the number of prior forecasting calls available at inference, or compare against a baseline that simply concatenates longer history into a one-shot model. This would help establish whether the benefit comes from recurrent state propagation per se, rather than just access to more temporal context.

The multi-agent results are encouraging, but the treatment is somewhat superficial. The paper claims that the method is not integrated with specialized multi-agent designs yet still performs well. However, the architecture description remains largely single-agent-centric, especially in the trajectory memory bank discussion. It would be helpful to explain how the scene-context stream and trajectory stream scale with the number of queried agents, whether memory is maintained independently per agent, and what the computational complexity is in dense scenes. Without this, the multi-agent contribution feels more like an additional benchmark result than a fully supported claim.

There are also several writing and presentation issues that reduce clarity. The paper contains grammatical errors and awkward phrasing throughout. Some examples include “we anticipate to address,” “first introduce,” “the future motion patterns involves,” and inconsistent capitalization and terminology. Figure and table references are occasionally confusing, and Figure 1 appears duplicated later in the paper. Table 5 is referred to as “Tab. 3(b)” in the text, which is clearly an editing mistake. These issues are fixable, but for a top-tier venue the paper would benefit from careful proofreading and tighter exposition.

I also think the paper should be more explicit about what exactly RealMotion-I is. It is described as an independent variant without data reorganization and stream modules, but it also appears to use a different architecture from some external baselines and a much smaller parameter count. If RealMotion-I is the main internal control, then its architecture, training recipe, and relation to the full model should be described very clearly. Otherwise, it is hard to know whether the gains are due to continuity modeling or simply due to a stronger/smaller base architecture.

A few concrete experiments would substantially strengthen the paper. First, compare against a baseline trained on the reorganized continuous data but evaluated independently, with matched optimization budget, to isolate the effect of data reorganization from temporal state propagation. Second, compare against a baseline that uses longer concatenated history in a one-shot model, to test whether recurrence is necessary. Third, report metrics across all sub-scenes in a sequence, not only the final one, including temporal consistency measures. Fourth, analyze failure cases of the trajectory memory bank, especially error accumulation and mode collapse over time. Fifth, provide a more direct comparison to prior streaming forecasting work under a similar protocol if possible.

In terms of significance, I think the paper is directionally important. The community should indeed think more seriously about continuous forecasting rather than isolated snapshots. The proposed framework is plausible and empirically strong. But for a top-tier conference, I would expect a cleaner disentangling of contributions, stronger methodological clarity, and more rigorous evaluation of the continuous setting itself. Right now, the paper demonstrates that a particular combination of data reorganization and lightweight temporal propagation improves benchmark performance, but it does not yet fully establish the broader claims about continuous driving as convincingly as it could.

My overall assessment is moderately positive but with reservations. The paper has a strong motivation, promising empirical results, and a practically relevant perspective. Its main weaknesses are fairness and interpretability of comparisons, incomplete positioning relative to prior streaming work, and insufficiently controlled evidence for which component is truly responsible for the gains. If these issues were addressed, I would view the work much more favorably.

I would recommend acceptance only if the venue is willing to reward strong practical framing and empirical performance despite some experimental and clarity shortcomings. Otherwise, this is closer to a borderline paper that needs a more rigorous treatment of the continuous evaluation setting and stronger controlled baselines.

The main strengths are the practical problem formulation, the intuitive two-stream temporal design, strong empirical gains over the internal baseline, and a useful efficiency discussion. The main weaknesses are unclear novelty relative to prior streaming forecasting, confounding introduced by data reorganization, insufficiently controlled comparisons, limited evaluation of temporal consistency over full sequences, and several presentation issues.

For improvement, I strongly encourage the authors to: sharpen the distinction from prior streaming/temporal forecasting; add matched-control baselines for reorganized data and training budget; clarify identity handling, memory bank mechanics, and alignment across changing scene sets; evaluate sequence-level forecasting quality over all sub-scenes; and revise the writing carefully for clarity and correctness.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes RealMotion, a motion forecasting framework for continuous driving that departs from the standard independent-scene formulation. The method reorganizes benchmark data into sequences of sub-scenes, then uses two temporal modules: a scene context stream that propagates historical scene features via cross-attention after coordinate alignment, and an agent trajectory stream that stores past predicted trajectories/features in a memory bank and refines current predictions using trajectory-conditioned attention. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2, including single-agent and multi-agent settings, report strong leaderboard results and ablations suggesting gains from the continuous-data formulation and both temporal streams.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment: forecasting is naturally sequential/continuous rather than isolated per scene.
The proposed framework is conceptually clear, with two complementary temporal mechanisms: scene-level context accumulation and trajectory-level prediction relaying.
Empirical results on Argoverse 2 test leaderboard are strong, including improvements over QCNet on several metrics, and the paper also reports multi-agent results.

Ablation studies cover the main components (data reorganization, scene context stream, agent trajectory stream, alignment, trajectory embedding, depth, split points), which helps support the design choices.
The method appears relatively parameter-efficient compared with some baselines, and the paper discusses online/offline latency considerations.
weaknesses: The central experimental claim is weakened by the fact that the proposed setting changes the data formulation itself; comparisons against prior methods are largely not apples-to-apples because most baselines are evaluated in the standard independent-scene benchmark setting rather than under the same reorganized continuous protocol.

The data reorganization strategy may introduce overlap and information redundancy between training/evaluation sub-scenes, but the paper does not rigorously analyze whether this changes task difficulty or creates favorable temporal leakage relative to standard forecasting assumptions.

Methodological details are underspecified in several places, including how agents/maps are associated across sub-scenes, how missing/appearing/disappearing agents are handled, memory bank retrieval policy, and exact online inference protocol.

The claimed practical relevance is only partially validated because experiments are still conducted on retrospectively reorganized offline datasets rather than a true streaming benchmark or closed-loop autonomous driving stack.

The gains on some key multimodal metrics are modest, and the strongest improvements are on single-mode metrics, which may indicate the method mainly smooths/refines predictions rather than fundamentally improving multimodal future uncertainty modeling.
The paper lacks stronger comparisons to prior temporal/streaming forecasting work, especially the cited streaming benchmark paper, under matched settings.
methodological_flaws: Potential fairness issue in empirical comparison: RealMotion is trained/evaluated with reorganized sequential inputs, while most leaderboard baselines were developed for the original benchmark protocol. This makes the reported state-of-the-art claim scientifically weaker unless baselines are re-run under the same continuous data structure or RealMotion is also evaluated strictly under the original protocol without extra sequential context.

Possible train/test distribution alteration from data reorganization is not rigorously justified. Splitting one scene into multiple overlapping sub-scenes can effectively augment data and may reduce difficulty by exposing highly correlated contexts; the paper does not quantify overlap effects or rule out inflated gains from redundancy.

Equation (3) and the trajectory alignment description are mathematically unclear. The transform uses the current heading angle rather than an explicitly defined relative rotation between historical and current frames, and the notation for origin selection via y_i[Δt·q] is ambiguous when Δt varies or indexing is non-integer. This weakens confidence in the correctness/reproducibility of the trajectory relaying mechanism.

The scene-context alignment in Eq. (1) relies on MLN with pose/time encoding, but this is not a geometric transformation. It is not demonstrated that such feature-level conditioning is sufficient for accurate cross-scene correspondence, especially for dynamic agents and changing local neighborhoods.

The memory bank stores past predicted trajectories rather than ground truth during inference/training, which can propagate model errors over time. The paper does not provide a dedicated analysis of error accumulation, robustness to bad early predictions, or long-horizon degradation.

Latency comparison is not fully rigorous: RealMotion offline uses three passes because of the reorganized sequence, while online numbers are discussed separately and not directly benchmarked against all baselines under identical implementation/caching assumptions. Thus the efficiency claim is suggestive rather than conclusive.
